Weather

Continuous voice forecasts and alerts, plus the satellites that send pictures. Weather radio is the easiest place to hear a real signal immediately.

NOAA WX 7

162.550 MHz · NFM · 12.5 kHz

The US weather radio network repeats forecasts, watches, and warnings around the clock. Channel 7 is the primary frequency in many areas.

Listen forA synthesized voice cycling the local forecast; alerts interrupt the loop.

WXUS

NOAA WX 2

162.425 MHz · NFM · 12.5 kHz

One of the seven NOAA weather radio channels. Which channel carries your local transmitter depends on where you are.

Listen forThe same forecast loop as channel 7, often from a different transmitter.

WXUS

NOAA WX 5

162.475 MHz · NFM · 12.5 kHz

Another NOAA weather channel. Scanning 162.400–162.550 is the quickest way to find the strongest local transmitter.

Listen forA weather loop with different signal strength and possibly different coverage.

WXUS

Emergency

Channels reserved for distress, safety, and shared public use. Long silence is normal; that is what makes a transmission stand out.

Guard

121.500 MHz · AM · 25 kHz

The international aviation emergency frequency. Silence is the normal state; a transmission is exceptional.

Listen forBrief AM voice, an ELT sweep, or nothing at all.

EMRGLOBAL

Marine 16

156.800 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

VHF marine channel 16 is reserved for distress, safety, and calling. Most traffic is short and procedural.

Listen forCoast guard broadcasts, bridge calls, and radio checks.

SEAGLOBAL

GMRS 462

462.675 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

US GMRS/FRS channels carry family, off-road, and neighborhood traffic. Repeater use varies by license and location.

Listen forShort FM voice bursts, often with a CTCSS tone or a repeater tail.

EMRUS

Satellites

Short passes carrying images, telemetry, and occasional voice. These need a clear view of the sky and patience between passes.

NOAA APT

137.100 MHz · WFM · 200 kHz

NOAA polar satellites send slow-scan weather images on VHF. Passes last minutes and the signal moves quickly.

Listen forA warbling APT tone; software turns it into a grayscale cloud image.

IMGGLOBAL

GOES HRIT

1694.100 MHz · USB · 200 kHz

Geostationary weather satellites downlink higher-rate imagery in L-band. This needs a dish and a decoder more than a casual whip.

Listen forA wide digital signal; no voice, and usually no decode without the right antenna.

IMGGLOBAL

ISS Voice

145.800 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

The International Space Station sometimes transmits voice and packet on the amateur 2m band during a pass.

Listen forShort voice contacts or APRS packet bursts while the station is overhead.

HAMGLOBAL

Data & LoRa

APRS, MeshCore, LoRa, ISM sensors, and digital weak-signal modes. Expect chirps and bursts rather than a voice you can listen to.

APRS

144.390 MHz · NFM · 12.5 kHz

APRS carries position, weather, and short telemetry on 1200-baud AFSK. The frequency is regional; 144.390 is common in North America.

Listen forBrief data bursts every few minutes from nearby trackers and digipeaters.

DATAGLOBAL

MeshCore

915.000 MHz · NFM · 125 kHz

MeshCore uses LoRa packet radio for off-grid text, telemetry, and mesh routing. It is not a voice service.

Listen forChirpy LoRa bursts and short packets; a mesh client is needed to read them.

DATAUS

LoRa 868

868.100 MHz · NFM · 125 kHz

European ISM LoRa gateways and sensors use 868 MHz. Duty cycle and regional rules shape how often they transmit.

Listen forLong chirps with quiet gaps; decoders are needed to recover payloads.

DATAEU

ISM 433

433.920 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

433 MHz is crowded with remotes, weather sensors, tire sensors, and keyfobs. Most packets are very short.

Listen forTiny digital chirps and repeated sensor bursts, not continuous audio.

DATAGLOBAL

40m FT8

7.074 MHz · USB · 3 kHz

FT8 is a narrow digital mode for weak-signal contacts. It packs a contact into 15-second sequences.

Listen forA rhythmic sequence of tones, repeating in 15-second slots.

DATAGLOBAL

Aviation

AM voice around airports, plus 1090 MHz surveillance. Airband is line-of-sight and busiest near an airport.

Tower

118.000 MHz · AM · 25 kHz

Airband tower and ground frequencies sit just above 118 MHz. Exact assignments vary by airport.

Listen forClipped AM voice: clearances, taxi instructions, and readbacks.

AIRGLOBAL

ATIS

135.000 MHz · AM · 25 kHz

ATIS is a recorded airport information loop with weather and runway status. Frequencies vary by airport.

Listen forA steady recorded voice repeating weather and airport conditions.

AIRGLOBAL

ADS-B

1090.000 MHz · AM · 200 kHz

Aircraft broadcast identity, position, and altitude on 1090 MHz. It is a data signal, not voice.

Listen forShort pulses from many aircraft; a decoder turns them into a live map.

DATAGLOBAL

Marine

VHF marine channels and AIS ship tracking. Range is usually local unless you have height and a good antenna.

AIS 1

161.975 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

Ships and shore stations exchange identity, position, and course over AIS. Channel 1 is one of two AIS frequencies.

Listen forShort digital bursts; a decoder shows vessels on a map.

DATAGLOBAL

AIS 2

162.025 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

The second AIS channel. Larger harbors may use both channels heavily.

Listen forThe same ship-tracking bursts as AIS 1, often from different vessels.

DATAGLOBAL

Broadcast

Wide commercial signals: FM radio and digital television. These are strong, continuous, and easy to tune by ear or eye.

FM 90.3

90.300 MHz · WFM · 200 kHz

A typical FM broadcast frequency. Commercial stations are continuous and very strong compared with the signals above.

Listen forMusic, ads, and DJ talk; the receiver should sound immediately intelligible.

FMUS

FM 98.1

98.100 MHz · WFM · 200 kHz

Another FM broadcast example. Use the band map as a starting point, then scan nearby for a stronger station.

Listen forA different music or talk format; stereo pilot tones may be visible in the spectrum.

FMUS

ATSC 533

533.000 MHz · AM · 200 kHz

A US digital television channel example. ATSC occupies a 6 MHz block and carries several subchannels.

Listen forA wide noisy-looking block that a TV tuner turns into video and audio.

TVUS

Amateur

Calling frequencies and digital watering holes used by licensed operators. Activity follows time of day and propagation.

2m Call

146.520 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

The national 2m calling frequency in the US and a common simplex meeting place elsewhere. Activity is local and informal.

Listen forShort FM voice contacts; move to another simplex frequency to continue.

HAMGLOBAL

70cm Call

446.000 MHz · NFM · 25 kHz

A common 70cm calling frequency. Local repeater and simplex activity varies a lot by city.

Listen forShort FM voice contacts, repeater IDs, or silence.

HAMGLOBAL
Frequencies are starting points. Antenna, location, and time of day decide what is actually audible.
